claim: Solar irradiation including ultraviolet (UV) light causes tissue damage by generating reactive free radicals that can be electrophilic or nucleophilic due to unpaired electrons.
source: Solar irradiation including ultraviolet (UV) light causes tissue damage by generating reactive free radicals that can be electrophilic or nucleophilic due to unpaired electrons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about solar radiation effects.

claim: Drosophila TRPA1 was previously known only as an electrophile receptor.
source: We discover that Drosophila Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin 1 (TRPA1), previously known only as an electrophile receptor, sensitively detects photochemically active sunlight through nucleophile sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as prior knowledge about TRPA1.

claim: Drosophila TRPA1 sensitively detects photochemically active sunlight through nucleophile sensitivity.
source: We discover that Drosophila Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin 1 (TRPA1), previously known only as an electrophile receptor, sensitively detects photochemically active sunlight through nucleophile sensitivity.
evidence: This is the main discovery claim stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Rapid light-dependent feeding deterrence in Drosophila was mediated only by the TRPA1(A) isoform.
source: Rapid light-dependent feeding deterrence in Drosophila was mediated only by the TRPA1(A) isoform, despite the TRPA1(A) and TRPA1(B) isoforms having similar electrophile sensitivities.

claim: TRPA1(A) and TRPA1(B) isoforms have similar electrophile sensitivities.

evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3a showing similar NMM responses.

claim: TRPA1(A) isoform dependence re-emerges in the detection of structurally varied nucleophilic compounds.
source: Such isoform dependence re-emerges in the detection of structurally varied nucleophilic compounds and nucleophilicity-accompanying hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
evidence: This is supported by data showing responses to DTT, imidazole, and BTC in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: TRPA1(A) isoform dependence re-emerges in the detection of nucleophilicity-accompanying hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).

claim: Isoform-dependent mechanisms require a common set of TRPA1(A)-specific residues dispensable for electrophile detection.

evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data in Figure 4 showing C105A and R113A/R116A mutations.

claim: TRPA1(A) rapidly responds to natural sunlight intensities through its nucleophile sensitivity as a receptor of photochemically generated radicals.
source: Collectively, TRPA1(A) rapidly responds to natural sunlight intensities through its nucleophile sensitivity as a receptor of photochemically generated radicals, leading to an acute light-induced behavioral shift in Drosophila.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: TRPA1(A) activation leads to an acute light-induced behavioral shift in Drosophila.
source: Collectively, TRPA1(A) rapidly responds to natural sunlight intensities through its nucleophile sensitivity as a receptor of photochemically generated radicals, leading to an acute light-induced behavioral shift in Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by feeding deterrence data in Figures 1 and 6.

claim: TRPA1 is the only conserved reactive chemical receptor in the bilateria from humans to flies.
source: TRPA1 is the only conserved reactive chemical receptor in the bilateria from humans to flies (Kang et al., 2010), and is activated rather than inactivated by covalent modification unlike most proteins (Macpherson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: TRPA1 is activated rather than inactivated by covalent modification unlike most proteins.

claim: Only electrophilicity has been shown to provoke TRPA1-dependent nociception.

source: The two resulting TRPA1 channel isoforms, TRPA1(A) and TRPA1(B), differ only in their N-termini, and share more than 90% of their primary structure.

claim: TRPA1(A)-positive cells can reliably detect reactive chemicals regardless of fluctuations in ambient temperature.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Kang et al., 2012.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation context.

claim: TRPA1(B) is expressed in internal AC neurons that direct TrpA1-dependent long-term thermotaxis of the animal.

claim: Mammalian TRPA1 requires an extremely high UV intensity (580 mW/cm2) for direct activation.
source: Despite its electrophile sensitivity, mammalian TRPA1 requires an extremely high UV intensity (580 mW/cm2) for direct activation (Hill and Schaefer, 2009), which is at least 4-fold greater than the extraterrestrial solar constant (SC: the total solar irradiation density measured by a satellite, 137 mW/cm2 [Gueymard, 2004]).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Hill and Schaefer, 2009.

claim: The UV intensity required for mammalian TRPA1 activation is at least 4-fold greater than the extraterrestrial solar constant.
source: Despite its electrophile sensitivity, mammalian TRPA1 requires an extremely high UV intensity (580 mW/cm2) for direct activation (Hill and Schaefer, 2009), which is at least 4-fold greater than the extraterrestrial solar constant (SC: the total solar irradiation density measured by a satellite, 137 mW/cm2 [Gueymard, 2004]).

claim: Electrophilic sensitivity is inadequate for sensitive detection of photochemically-produced free radicals.
source: The high UV intensity requirement for TRPA1 activation in mammals indicates that electrophilic sensitivity is inadequate for sensitive detection of photochemically-produced free radicals, although radicals are often regarded as inflicting electrophilic oxidative stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high UV intensity requirement for mammalian TRPA1.

claim: Drosophila TRPA1 readily responds to UV and H2O2.

source: Insects and birds are able to visualize upper-UV wavelengths (above 320 nm) via UV-specific rhodopsins (Salcedo et al., 2003; Ödeen and Håstad, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

source: Visual detection of UV in this range by insects generally elicits attraction towards the UV source rather than avoidance (Craig and Bernard, 1990; Washington, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Lower UV wavelengths, such as UVB (280–315 nm) at natural intensities, decrease insect phytophagy.
source: At the same time, lower UV wavelengths, such as UVB (280–315 nm) at natural intensities, have been known to decrease insect phytophagy (Zavala et al., 2001; Rousseaux et al., 1998) via a direct effect on the animals that does not involve the visual system (Mazza et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: UVB-induced decrease in insect phytophagy occurs via a direct effect on the animals that does not involve the visual system.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Mazza et al., 1999.

claim: UV illumination at 5.2 mW/cm2 rapidly elicited firing of single taste neurons in i-a bristles.
source: Illumination of 295 nm UV light at an intensity of 5.2 mW/cm2(~85% of the total UV intensity on the ground [6.1 mW/cm2]) received by the fly labellum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, b, d) rapidly elicited firing of single taste neurons in i-a bristles which was sustained after illumination (Figure 1a, b).

claim: UV-evoked firing in i-a bristles was sustained after illumination.
source: Illumination of 295 nm UV light at an intensity of 5.2 mW/cm2(~85% of the total UV intensity on the ground [6.1 mW/cm2]) received by the fly labellum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, b, d) rapidly elicited firing of single taste neurons in i-a bristles which was sustained after illumination (Figure 1a, b).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1a, b.

claim: TrpA1ins mutant flies showed severely reduced UV response in i-bristles.
source: Interestingly, TrpA1ins showed an severely reduced UV response in i-bristles, suggesting the importance of TrpA1 for UV sensing in these sensilla (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1a, b.

claim: UV illumination at ~1.3 mW/cm2 substantially decreased the feeding of wild-type flies.

claim: UV illumination did not disrupt the feeding of TrpA1ins mutants.

evidence: This is supported by feeding assay data shown in Figure 1d, e.

claim: TrpA1- and UV-dependent spikings in aversive taste neurons suppress food ingestion.

evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between UV-evoked neuronal activity and feeding behavior.

claim: Reintroduction of TrpA1(A) cDNA to Gr66a-Gal4 bitter cells restored UV-induced feeding deterrence in TrpA1ins.
source: However, reintroduction of either TrpA1(A) and TrpA1(B) cDNA to Gr66a-Gal4 bitter cells resulted in differential restoration of UV-induced feeding deterrence in TrpA1ins (Figure 1f).

evidence: This is supported by feeding assay data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: TrpA1(A) expression in TrpA1ins i-bristle bitter neurons generated robust action potentials in response to UV illumination.
source: In sensillum recordings, TrpA1(B) expression in TrpA1ins i-bristle bitter neurons produced very few UV-evoked spikes, while TrpA1(A) expression generated robust action potentials in response to UV illumination (Figure 1g,h and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1g, h.

claim: The 2.5-minute-long UV illumination used in the feeding assays raised the temperature in the vials by 1.6 ± 0.07°C with active cooling.
source: Indeed, the 2.5-minute-long UV illumination used in the feeding assays raised the temperature in the vials by 1.6 ± 0.07°C and 3.25 ± 0.13°C with and without active cooling, respectively, at ambient temperatures between 22.5 and 23°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is supported by temperature measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The 2.5-minute-long UV illumination used in the feeding assays raised the temperature in the vials by 3.25 ± 0.13°C without active cooling.

claim: The mild UV-dependent feeding deterrence induced by TrpA1(B) in TrpA1ins animals resulted from the high thermosensitivity of TRPA1(B).

evidence: This is an inference based on the temperature sensitivity data.

claim: Gr5a neurons expressing TrpA1(A) but not those expressing TrpA1(B) showed robust UV-induced firing.
source: Similar to the results from Gr66a-Gal4 cells, Gr5a neurons expressing TrpA1(A) but not those expressing TrpA1(B) showed robust UV-induced firing (Figure 2a,b), although, unlike bitter-sensing neurons, UV-evoked firing in Gr5a neurons was attenuated soon after the removal of illumination (Figures 1g and 2a).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2a, b.

claim: UV-evoked firing in Gr5a neurons was attenuated soon after the removal of illumination.

evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 1g and 2a.

claim: TRPA1(A) is capable of responding to UV light without the co-expression of other signaling factors such as GPCRs.
source: These results suggest that TRPA1(A) is capable of responding to UV light without the co-expression of other signaling factors such as GPCRs, as the intrinsic molecular thermosensor TRPA1(B) independently reacts to IR, which warms TRPA1(B)-expressing cells (Kang et al., 2012).

claim: Heterologous Xenopus oocytes expressing TRPA1(A) but not those expressing TRPA1(B) showed TRPA1-dependent current increases in response to 295 nm UV light at 3.8 mW/cm2.
source: In line with the observation that Drosophila TRPA1(A) confers a low threshold of UV responsiveness in nonnative cells, heterologous Xenopus oocytes expressing TRPA1(A) but not those expressing TRPA1(B) showed TRPA1-dependent current increases in response to 295 nm UV light at ~62% of the total ground UV intensity, 3.8 mW/cm2 (Figure 2d–f; for an estimation of UV irradiance received by oocytes see Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2d-f.

claim: The UV-induced current in TRPA1(A)-expressing oocytes exhibited the reversal potential and outward rectification previously associated with currents recorded from fly TRPA1.
source: The UV-induced current exhibited the reversal potential and outward rectification previously associated with currents recorded from fly TRPA1 (Kang et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data and comparison with prior work.

claim: The UV and NMM responses serially recorded from each TRPA1(A)-expressing cell showed similar reversal potentials of −5.6 ± 1.1 and −5.4 ± 1.0 mV, respectively.
source: The UV and NMM responses serially recorded from each cell showed similar reversal potentials of −5.6 ± 1.1 and −5.4 ± 1.0 mV, respectively (not significantly different, paired t-test, n = 7).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: Inside-out macropatches from TRPA1-expressing oocytes responded to UV light in an isoform-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, inside-out macropatches from TRPA1-expressing oocytes also responded to UV light in an isoform-dependent manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,b,e).

claim: WT but not TrpA1ins animals showed NMM-dependent feeding avoidance.

evidence: This is supported by feeding assay data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The isoforms TRPA1(A) and TRPA1(B) are similar in their ability to confer electrophile responsiveness in vivo.
source: The reintroduction of either TrpA1(A) or TrpA1(B) cDNA similarly restored NMM-dependent feeding avoidance in TrpA1ins, demonstrating that the isoforms are similar in their ability to confer electrophile responsiveness in vivo.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Danen and Warner, 1977.

claim: TrpA1(A)R113A/R116A mutant has a specific dominant negative effect on TRPA1(A)-mediated H2O2 and UV detection in vivo.

claim: TrpA1-positive neurons are necessary for UV-dependent feeding avoidance.

claim: Imidazole and benzyl thiocyanate (BTC) preferentially activated agTRPA1(A) over agTRPA1(B).

claim: TRPA1(A) responds to nucleophilicity and not the structures of the compounds.
source: Other structurally distinct nucleophiles, such as imidazole and benzyl thiocyanate (BTC), also preferentially activated agTRPA1(A) over agTRPA1(B) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), demonstrating that TRPA1(A) responds to nucleophilicity and not the structures of the compounds.

claim: UV responses from agTRPA1(A) were ~5 times higher than those from Drosophila TRPA1(A) tested at the same settings.
